sources.title: The Cost of Sequencing a Human Genome

facts.text: The Human Genome Project began in October 1990 and was completed in April 2003, two years ahead of its planned 2005 finish.
The project’s central goal was to produce the first sequence of the human genome, a reference of about 3 billion bases, the chemical letters A, C, G and T.

The project took about 13 years instead of the planned 15 and involved researchers at 20 universities and research centers in six countries: the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan and China.

The project was originally expected to cost $3 billion, and most agree the final cost was close to that; total US funding of about $2.7 billion also paid for technology development, mapping and work on other organisms besides sequencing the human genome.
Producing that first human genome sequence alone is estimated to have cost between $500 million and $1 billion.
The draft sequence announced in June 2000 covered about 90 percent of the genome; the April 2003 sequence covered about 92 percent and still had fewer than 400 gaps.
On 31 March 2022, the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium filled the remaining gaps and produced the first truly complete human genome sequence.
The reference sequence came from several anonymous volunteers: about 70 percent from one person and the rest from 19 others.
NHGRI has tracked the cost of DNA sequencing at the centers it funds; its cost per genome assumes a human-sized genome of 3,000 megabases.
From 2001 to October 2007 the centers used older Sanger-based machines; from January 2008 they switched to next-generation machines, and costs then began falling much faster than before.
NHGRI’s cost figures include labor, equipment, chemicals and first-step data processing, but not later analysis such as assembling sequences, finding variants and interpreting results.
A person’s own genome has about 6 billion bases, because people carry two copies of almost all their DNA, one from each parent.
Researchers, institutions and companies count sequencing costs in different ways, and the price a company charges may be higher or lower than its actual cost.
Genomic medicine, the use of a person’s genomic information in their medical care, is already affecting cancer care, drug treatment, rare and undiagnosed diseases, and infectious disease.
It is often estimated that turning a new research finding into routine medical practice takes 17 years on average.
In the dataset, the cost per genome fell from about $61.4 million in 2002 to about $525 in 2022, more than 100,000 times lower.
In the dataset, the 2010 cost (about $29,092) was less than one-thousandth of the 2002 cost (about $61.4 million).
In two-year steps from 2002 to 2022, the largest drop in dollars came between 2002 and 2004, about $42.9 million.
In two-year steps, the cost fell about 31 times between 2006 and 2008 and about 12 times between 2008 and 2010.
In the dataset, the cost rose from 2016 to 2018 and again from 2020 to 2022.
